name: HELVIPAD
description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from video sequences across diverse environments, including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions. Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images.

creator.name: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi

citeAs: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi. HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335v2 [cs.CV], 2025.
rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a vertical top-bottom arrangement with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. The rig was mounted on a custom-built, remotely controlled robot chassis. Data collection took place across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus.
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels. The ratio of labeled pixels is increased from 12% to 61% through depth completion.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of equirectangular images captured by two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras at 30 fps with an initial resolution of 3840 × 1920 pixels, and LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor operating at 10 fps with 64 beams. Data were collected on a university campus between December 2023 and February 2024.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR point clouds are projected onto equirectangular images through a calibration process involving initial rotation and translation transformations, conversion to spherical coordinates, and optimization of rotation and translation parameters by minimizing the error between projected points and their corresponding locations on equirectangular images. Disparity values are obtained from depth values using the equation: d = arctan(sin(θb) / (rbottom/Bcamera - cos(θb))), where θb denotes the polar angle, rbottom is the depth, Bcamera the camera baseline, and d is the disparity in radians, converted to degrees.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are cropped to remove unnecessary borders (sky, ground) and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 pixels, resulting in a final resolution of 1920×512 pixels. To match the LiDAR's frame rate (10 fps), one out of every three camera frames is retained. A hardware-triggered synchronization method using an external flash lasting 33 ms is used to synchronize sensors, with a maximum potential de-synchronization of 16.67 ms across all sensors.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels are created by projecting LiDAR 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. An automated depth completion pipeline is applied to increase label density. The pipeline includes: (1) Temporal aggregation: aggregating the current frame's point cloud with those from the four preceding and four succeeding frames; (2) Interpolation: estimating depth for query points through a weighted average of k-nearest neighbors (k=17); (3) Filtering: filtering query points exceeding either an uncertainty criterion (relative weighted variance) or an out-of-distribution threshold (average distance to k-nearest neighbors exceeding approximately 0.37°) before mapping the remaining points to the image. The ratio of interpolated points after filtering is set to 80%.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To validate the depth completion pipeline, each LiDAR point cloud is split into training and test sets, and depth estimation metrics are computed on the test set. The pipeline significantly increases the ratio of labeled pixels from 12% to 61% while maintaining very low error rates. The average pixel error for LiDAR-to-image projection is 1.7 pixels for randomly selected points and 8.0 pixels for points from visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor for depth measurement; custom depth completion pipeline for label augmentation; KISS-ICP for LiDAR odometry (evaluated but not used in final pipeline)
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes recordings of pedestrians in indoor and outdoor environments, with an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences. No explicit discussion of demographic attributes or personally identifiable information is provided.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is designed to help build accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments, which are crucial for navigation and interaction in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, and agriculture. Mobile robots are increasingly used in these applications where accurate depth estimation is essential.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to scenes captured on a university campus. The depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars due to the temporal aggregation window. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact. The LiDAR's sparse point clouds result in labels covering only a fraction of total pixels before depth completion. The depth completion method does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries. Indoor-trained models show clear limitations in generalizing to outdoor scenes, particularly at night. The maximum potential de-synchronization across sensors is 16.67 ms.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, testing, and validation of omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models. It serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments. The dataset is suitable for applications requiring comprehensive spatial awareness, such as robotic navigation and exploration in complex indoor environments. The dataset includes a train-val set (20 sequences, 29,407 frames) and a test set (6 sequences, 10,146 frames), with both original and augmented (depth-completed) training data available.
